The `feature-factory:local-review` stage caps at 2 CLI passes: review → fix → verify-review.
But **the fix commit produced by the LAST pass is never itself reviewed.** On SMA-529 / PR 152,
pass 2 reviewed up to `0ae17b3`, I fixed its findings as `715777b`, and opened the PR — leaving
the final commit with no review at all from either the CLI or (thanks to a Fair-Usage rate limit)
the web bot.

That final unreviewed commit is not low-risk: on SMA-529 it was the one that added the
`_cmd_refresh` round-trip validation, and the follow-up pass over it found **5 more findings**,
including a genuine interaction bug the previous fix had introduced (a local-vs-UTC date basis
that made a European developer's `--refresh` stamp a date CI read as the future — which the
future-date guard, added in that same unreviewed commit, then rejected as corrupt).

**Why:** each fix round is new, unreviewed code, and the last one ships without a pass. A
"2 passes, done" cap silently means "n-1 commits reviewed".

**How to apply:** before opening the PR, run one more `coderabbit review --agent --base <base>`
over the whole branch — it is not rate limited, so a third pass costs ~2 minutes. Treat a fix
round's own commit as unreviewed until a pass has actually covered it. This is also the right
move when the web review is rate-limited (state 2 in
[[coderabbit-loop-inprogress-detector]]): the CLI is the bypass, and running it over the full
branch covers exactly the commits the web bot never saw.

Corollary for the fix loop generally: findings that arrive from a *later* pass over an *earlier*
fix are the highest-value ones, because they catch defects introduced by fixing something else.
Do not treat "the reviewer already looked at this file" as coverage of a change made afterwards.

{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"ADR-0028: Always-on agent host — Postgres durability, inbox lease, CloudEvents envelope","url":"https://app.notion.com/p/41c830e8fbaa810fbf43d7912042d5ca?pvs=204","text":"Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/41c830e8fbaa810fbf43d7912042d5ca as of 2026-11-18T19:04:36.657Z: {"title":"ADR-0028: Always-on agent host — Postgres durability, inbox lease, CloudEvents envelope"} null Status: Proposed Date: 2026-11-18 Decided by: Sven Maschek Issue: [SMA-785](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-785/adr-always-on-agent-host-durability-substrate-worker-model-event) Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-18-sma-785-agent-host-adr-design.md (paigasus-core, SMA-785) Builds on: ADR-0005, ADR-0006, ADR-0014, ADR-0016 ## Context - The article's model. Every trigger goes into a durable inbox. One worker per inbox merges the pending events into one run. Timers live in a separate store and never start runs. A scheduler turns due timers into inbox events. A run ends in one of three ways: send a message, send nothing, or defer a tool call for approval. - IAM already uses most of this pattern. ADR-0016: a Postgres transactional outbox (event_outbox, with attempts and parked), a relay that drains with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, NATS JetStream, and a CloudEvents 1.0 JSON envelope (rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/adapters/events/cloud_event.rs, extensions schemaversion, actorprn, correlationid). IAM uses SeaORM 2 with sea-orm-migration. - Helikon is a separate public repo (paigasus-helikon, published to [crates.io](http://crates.io)). The host depends on the published crates. Facts that this ADR builds on (verified in the code): - Sessions are an append-only SessionEvent log behind the Session trait (append, events, snapshot). A session id is a plain String. - TokioRunner calls snapshot() once at run start and append() once at finalize, also on a failed, cancelled or timed-out run. Persistence is best-effort: an append error is logged, not returned. run_streamed does not finalize on a natural end without a terminal event. - SessionRecorder::drain writes a synthetic result for every unmatched ToolCalled. It records the run input and four AgentEvent kinds only. Items that the loop adds to its own conversation are not recorded. - PermissionDecision is Allow | Deny | AskUser | Replace. Guard rules can return Ask. Both AskUser and guard Ask block the loop on an ApprovalHandler future. ApprovalOutcome is only Allow | Deny. LoopState::NeedsApproval exists and returns NotImplemented. - PreToolUse hooks run before authorisation and can replace the args. Replace can too. - The only mid-run control is a CancellationToken. Input guardrails run once, on the seed input. A hook can return InjectSystemMessage. Nothing can inject a user-role message. - CompactingSession compacts inside append, with a model call that nothing can cancel. Its summary is a SessionEvent::Compacted, which project() renders as Item::System. - TemporalRunner (runtime-temporal 0.5.3, Temporal Rust SDK 1.0) is implemented. Its v0 rejects hooks, guardrails and handoffs. - sessions-testkit (the Session conformance suite) has publish = false. - Helikon ADR-6: durability is a seam (Runner), not built in. - IAM has no delegation mechanism. A service cannot act for a principal today. Goals and anti-goals - Goal: one durability model for the inbox, timers, leases, runs, threads, sessions and the outbox. - Goal: at most one committed run per lease token, provable from the data. A run that lost its lease is cancelled at once and never commits. - Goal: one event envelope for every event that enters or leaves the host. - Goal: a rule that says, for every run, whether it resumes a session or starts a fresh one. - Goal: a deferred tool call that ends the run cleanly and resumes later. - Goal: a safe way for an event that arrives during a run to join that run, or to stop it. - Goal: a clear line between the open core and paigasus-cloud. - Non-goal: multi-agent coordination across inboxes (out of scope for v1, per the project description). - Non-goal: exactly-once delivery. The host is at-least-once with deduplication, like ADR-0016. - Non-goal: a Temporal adapter. The ADR keeps it possible. It does not build it. - Non-goal: a decision on how an agent holds a principal's access. See decision (k). - Anti-goal: the design fails, even if it works, if a self-hoster needs a Temporal cluster to run the core. - Anti-goal: untrusted content reaches the model in the system role (decision (n) lists every path). - Anti-goal: a crashed run sends half a message, or loses an event. - Anti-goal: two runs commit for the same inbox under the same lease. - Anti-goal: a party other than an authorised approver can approve a deferred call. ## Decision ### (a) Durability substrate: Postgres is the source of truth - The host's Postgres database holds every durable record: inbox, inbox_event, inbox_lease, run, thread, session_event, pending_tool_call, timer, outbox_message, and the Postgres memory store (SMA-789). - NATS is an ingress source (a JetStream consumer that writes inbox rows) and the fan-out for outbox events. It is never the source of truth for the inbox. - Redis is optional, for caches only. No correctness depends on it. - A Scheduler port in paigasus-agent-host-core turns due timers into inbox events (decision (l)). The core ships a Postgres adapter. A Temporal adapter can implement the same port later. - The core always runs Helikon's TokioRunner, through Runner::run, not run_streamed. The host does not wrap the loop in Temporal. Reason: TemporalRunner v0 rejects hooks, guardrails and handoffs, and the permission layer (SMA-793) needs hooks and guardrails. - Times that decide correctness (lease expiry, due timers, backoff) use the database clock (now(), or clock_timestamp() inside a transaction that can wait on a lock), never the worker clock. ### (b) Run lifecycle and the atomic commit Claim transaction (short, before the model loop): 1. Take the lease (decision (c)). 2. Select the claimable events of one thread (decision (f)). 3. Insert a run row: status running, the lease token, the claimed event ids. 4. Set claimed_run_id on those events and increment their attempts. Events keep the status pending. So a crash also counts as an attempt, and an expired lease frees the events with no reaper: an event whose claiming run is not running under a live lease is claimable again. No transaction or database connection stays open across the model loop. Commit transaction (one, at the end of the run), through a RunCommitter port in the domain (commit(RunOutcome, LeaseToken) -> Result), so the domain does not see SeaORM: 1. Lock the lease row (SELECT … FROM inbox_lease WHERE inbox_id = $1 FOR UPDATE) and check that token = $t AND expires_at > clock_timestamp(). clock_timestamp(), not now(), because now() is the start time of the transaction and the commit can wait on the lock. The lock serialises the commit with a lease take, which updates the same row. A matching token on an expired lease does not pass, even when no other worker has taken the lease yet. 2. UPDATE run SET status = WHERE id = $run AND status = 'running'. Zero rows, or a failed lease check in step 1, means "already committed, or lease lost". Roll back and discard. This also makes a retried commit (a lost COMMIT acknowledgement) harmless. 3. Append the run's session events (PgRunSession, below). 4. Insert or update the thread row (last_run_at). 5. Insert outbox messages. Insert new timers. Cancel timers the run cancelled (for example an approval expiry). 6. Insert or resolve pending_tool_call rows (decision (g)). 7. Write the buffered memory changes of the Postgres memory adapter. 8. Mark the claimed and folded inbox events done. Outcomes. completed, deferred, stopped, failed, discarded. - failed: the runner returned an error. The host classifies it: - transient (provider 429 or 5xx, a database error): roll back. The events get a not_before backoff and stay pending. - deterministic (max turns, a guardrail tripwire, invalid structured output, a provider 4xx, a timeout): commit only the run row with the error. The partial session events are discarded, so a malformed session cannot poison the thread. The events stay pending. - After max_attempts, the events move to dead. The console shows dead events and can replay them (SMA-799). - discarded: the lease was lost. Nothing commits. - Every run has a maximum wall time (RunConfig.timeout). - final_output is never delivered to the user. Only the send tool (SMA-792) sends messages. The host stores final_output on the run row. PgRunSession contract. The host implements Helikon's Session trait itself, because sessions-postgres writes through its own pool and its own transaction. - snapshot() reads the committed events of the thread's session and projects them (with the compaction rule in (f)). - append() only buffers in memory. It never fails. - events() and snapshot() return the committed events plus the buffer. - The commit writes the buffer. If the run is discarded, the buffer is dropped. - The host runs Helikon's sessions-testkit against PgRunSession. Helikon publishes the testkit with the release that carries (g) and (h). Side-effect guarantee, stated as it is. A run commits once, at the end. If a worker crashes at turn 10, the next attempt runs turns 1 to 10 again. The model can make new call_ids and different args. So a side-effect tool is at-least-once per run attempt, with possibly different args. A deferral does not prevent a repeat: an approved call runs before the commit of the resumed run, so a crash there runs it again. An approved call keeps its call_id across attempts, because the call_id comes from the deferred run's log. A tool that must not repeat keeps its own idempotency check, on the business key or on that call_id. Messages to the user go through the outbox, so a re-run never sends them twice. The dispatcher itself is at-least-once: a crash after a send and before the delivery record can send a message again. It passes the outbox message id as an idempotency key to channels that support one (SMA-792). A per-turn commit would bound the repeat to one turn. It is not chosen for v1 (see Alternatives considered). The S3 memory adapter cannot join the transaction. Its writes are at-least-once and can survive a discarded run. The Postgres memory adapter is the default. ### (c) Worker model: one lease per inbox - inbox_lease (inbox_id PK, holder, token BIGINT, expires_at). Lease rows are never deleted, so a token never repeats. - Take the lease. INSERT … ON CONFLICT (inbox_id) DO UPDATE SET token = inbox_lease.token + 1, holder = …, expires_at = now() + ttl WHERE inbox_lease.expires_at < now() RETURNING token. This also works for a new inbox that has no lease row. The candidate inbox is selected with the claimable predicate of (f), with FOR UPDATE OF inbox_lease SKIP LOCKED when the query joins inbox_event. - Heartbeat. UPDATE inbox_lease SET expires_at = clock_timestamp() + ttl WHERE inbox_id = $1 AND token = $t AND expires_at > clock_timestamp(). A heartbeat after expires_at does not revive the lease: zero rows means the lease is lost. lease_ttl is at least three heartbeat intervals. - Lease lost means: no successful heartbeat before expires_at. Zero rows updated and a database timeout both count, once expires_at has passed. On a lost lease the worker cancels the run at once with the CancellationToken and discards it. A cancel inside a tool call is no worse than the re-run that follows. - Interrupt. The run stops at the turn boundary (decision (h)), commits, keeps the lease, and claims again at once. Every claim under a held lease rotates the token first (UPDATE inbox_lease SET token = token + 1 … WHERE token = $t AND expires_at > clock_timestamp()), so the next run commits under a new token and the goal "at most one committed run per lease token" stays true. - One worker process serves many inboxes at the same time, up to a concurrency limit. ### (d) Inbox granularity, tenancy and routing - One inbox per (agent, principal). Split only when parallelism demands it (revisit trigger). - The inbox row holds the principal PRN. The org comes from the PRN (ADR-0014). Every query is scoped by the inbox. - An inbox is created explicitly, when an agent is bound to a principal. It is never created by the first event. - Routing. HTTP ingress names the inbox in the path (POST /v1/inboxes/{inbox}/events, SMA-787). Every other channel (a NATS subject, a webhook, an email address) has a channel configuration that maps it to exactly one inbox. An event that names no principal (for example an org-wide webhook) is routed by its channel configuration. A channel that cannot name one inbox is rejected at configuration time. - Ingress authorisation. Authentication alone does not let a caller write to an inbox. Before the insert, the host checks that the caller may write to the named inbox: a Cedar check through IAM (IsAuthorized, an agents action on the inbox resource) for HTTP ingress, and the channel binding for every other channel. A caller that fails the check gets 403, and no row is written. ### (e) Event envelope and ingress trust - Every inbox event, outbox message and approval reply is a CloudEvents 1.0 event in JSON structured mode (application/cloudevents+json), wire-compatible with IAM's cloud_event.rs (microsecond time, hyphenated id). - Extensions: schemaversion, actorprn, correlationid (as in IAM), and a new threadid. - data holds the proto3 JSON mapping of the agents/v1 message that type names. Events from outside (a raw webhook) carry their own JSON in data. type for events the host emits starts with agents. (for example agents.outbox.message). - Dedup. A unique constraint on (inbox_id, source, id). A duplicate insert is a success with no new row, and the handler returns 202. A duplicate whose payload differs is logged and counted. done rows are kept for a retention period, and that period is the dedup window. - The host, not the caller, sets the trust-bearing fields: - source comes from the authenticated channel configuration. - actorprn is the authenticated caller, set by the host. - A raw webhook without a CloudEvents id gets an id from the provider's delivery id, read from the header that the channel configuration names. A content hash is used only when the channel configuration selects it, for a provider whose identical payloads are always retries. Otherwise the host makes a new id, and that channel has no retry dedup. - A threadid is kept only if that thread belongs to the same inbox. Otherwise the host drops it, and the event starts a fresh thread. - Each channel configuration names how its caller is authenticated (an IAM API key, a webhook signature, a verified email sender). - The envelope code moves into a shared library crate (decision (j)). ### (f) Session policy: one run serves one thread - A thread is a sequence of runs on one Helikon session. The thread id is the Helikon session id. thread (id, inbox_id, created_at, last_run_at, closed). - Every outbox message carries the threadid of the run that sent it. A user reply carries it back (the channel adapter maps it, for example from email In-Reply-To). An approval reply carries the threadid of the deferred run. - A thread is live when it exists, is not closed, and its last_run_at is within the thread TTL. A thread with an open deferred call is always live. An operator can close a thread. - The claimable predicate. An event is claimable when its status is pending, not_before has passed, it is not claimed by a running run under a live lease, and one of these is true: - its thread has no open deferred call; - it resolves that thread's open call: an approval reply that matches an open call_id, the call's expiry timer event, or a user message on that thread (see (g), "superseded").

The predicate is used both to select an inbox and to claim events. The open-deferral state is a column on thread, written by the run commit, and indexed. So an inbox whose only pending events wait on an approval is idle and is not selected again.

- Claim. Take the oldest claimable event of the inbox (by received_at). - If it has a live threadid, claim the claimable events of that thread, in received_at order, up to the batch limit. The run resumes that thread. - If it has a threadid whose thread is not live, claim the claimable events with that same threadid, up to the batch limit. The run starts a fresh session under a new thread. Events of two different expired threads never share a run. - If it has no threadid (or the host dropped it, decision (e)), claim the claimable events that have no threadid, up to the batch limit. The run starts a fresh session under a new thread. - Events of other threads stay pending for the next claim. So several messages in one thread still produce one reply, and no run mixes threads. - A timer event with a threadid follows the same rule. If its thread is not live, it starts a fresh thread. - Compaction is a host step, not CompactingSession. After a commit, under the same lease, if the thread's token estimate is over a threshold and the thread has no open deferred call: 1. Run a memory-flush turn, so that facts that must persist go to memory (SMA-791). 2. Write a summary as a Compacted event, made by a separate model call that the host can cancel. 3. PgRunSession::snapshot() projects a Compacted event as a delimited user-role item and drops the events before it. It never projects it as a system item. ### (g) Deferred tool calls Helikon changes (on #[non_exhaustive] types; compile-compatible for callers): - PermissionDecision::Defer { prompt } and ApprovalOutcome::Defer, so that a policy, a guard Ask and an AskUser can all defer. The host's ApprovalHandler returns Defer. One deferral answers every ask point of one call. - The loop uses the existing LoopState::NeedsApproval. When a turn holds deferred calls, the loop runs the turn's other allowed calls, records their results, and ends the run at the turn boundary. - RunResult gets a stop reason: Completed | Deferred { calls: Vec } | Stopped { reason }. It also reaches run_streamed consumers and agrees with AgentEvent::is_terminal. - PendingToolCall and a new SessionEvent::ToolDeferred hold the call_id, the tool, the effective args (after PreToolUse and Replace), and the active agent (for a handoff). SessionRecorder::drain does not write a synthetic result for a deferred call. - A resume entry point takes resolutions (call_id → Approved | Denied { reason }). It writes the results of all resolved calls before any new input. On Approved it runs the call with the effective args, on the recorded agent: - It does not fire PreToolUse again. - It runs the deny rules, guard Deny, the mode and the policy again. - Defer, AskUser and guard Ask count as answered by this approval. - Any Deny wins. - A Replace that changes the args denies the call. - A tool that the agent no longer has is denied with "tool no longer available". - A Defer inside an AgentAsTool sub-run (depth > 0) is a Deny in v1. Its session is discarded, so there is nothing to resume. - A runner that does not support Defer (for example TemporalRunner v0) treats it as Deny. - Core's own matches without a wildcard (SessionEvent::kind, ts, project, tool_exec.rs) change with the new variants. Once a tool_deferred event is stored, the host cannot roll back below that Helikon version, because an older reader cannot parse the row. Host side (SMA-795): - The run commits with outcome deferred, inserts one pending_tool_call row per call (state open), sets the thread's open-deferral column, inserts one expiry timer per call, and releases the lease. - One ApprovalRequest per call goes through the outbox. It shows the effective args. It carries the threadid, the call_id, a hash of the effective args (RFC 8785 canonical JSON), and an approval token (below). - The thread resumes only when every open call of the deferred turn has a resolution. The first resolution per call_id wins (a unique constraint). A later reply is marked done with the outcome stale. The resolving commit cancels the expiry timer. - States. open → approved | denied | expired | superseded → resolved. - Expiry. The expiry timer resolves the call as Denied { reason: "approval expired" }. - Superseded. A user message on a thread with open calls resolves every open call as Denied { reason: "superseded by a new user message" }. The run then continues with that message after the denial results. So "cancel that" works at once, and a thread never waits for hours. - Who may approve (accepted at Gate 1): only the inbox principal in v1. The reply endpoint authenticates the approver through IAM and checks that the approver PRN is the inbox principal. The approval token is single-use and unguessable: an HMAC over inbox_id, thread_id, call_id, the args hash and the expiry. An email link carries the token, opens a confirmation page, and the approver signs in there. The token alone does not approve. Delegates and admin approvers come later, with (k). ### (h) Mid-run events: a turn-boundary checkpoint Helikon change: - An optional callback on RunContext, called at every turn boundary of the top-level loop and of handoff children: after all tool results of a turn are recorded, before the next model call. It is never called inside a tool call, in an AgentAsTool sub-run, or at a boundary where a call was deferred. - It returns Continue | Inject(Vec) | Stop { reason }. - Inject content is user content. The loop emits a new AgentEvent for it, and SessionRecorder records it as a UserMessage. So the thread history contains it. - The loop runs the input guardrails on injected content. A tripwire ends the run with Stop. - Stop ends the run at the boundary with stop reason Stopped. No tool call is half done. Host side: - At each boundary, one indexed query reads new claimable events of the running thread. The host claims them under the same lease and the same run. - Each agent definition has a mid-run policy per event type: queue (the default), fold or interrupt. Approval replies and expiry timer events always use queue. Events of other threads are never read at a boundary. - queue: the event stays pending for the next run. - fold: the host returns Inject. The event is marked done in the run commit. If the run is discarded, the event is claimable again. - interrupt: the host returns Stop, commits the run as stopped, keeps the lease, and starts a new run on the same thread with the new events. - An operator cancel from the console (SMA-799) also returns Stop. The run commits as stopped and keeps its work so far. - An interrupt that arrives during the last model call does not stop that turn's outbox messages. v1 has no extra check before the commit. This is a known limit. - A TemporalRunner would need the same checkpoint later, as a workflow signal. That is outside this ADR. ### (i) Open-core boundary Under ADR-0006 (a published-artifact dependency edge): - Core (paigasus-core, Apache-2.0): the inbox, timers, worker, outbox and dispatcher; the webhook and email channels; the Postgres and S3 memory adapters; the Postgres Scheduler adapter; the agents console zone. - paigasus-cloud: managed channel apps (Slack, Teams), hosted dreaming, and any managed Temporal adapter. They use the published crates and the agents/v1 protos. They never patch the core. ### (j) Crate layout The project description's layout stands, with these additions: - A new library crate for the CloudEvents envelope (the name is the builder's call, for example paigasus-cloudevents). It owns parse, validate and build, with extension attributes per service, and keeps IAM's wire bytes unchanged. IAM moves to it in a later issue. This ADR does not require that move. - paigasus-agent-host depends on the published paigasus-helikon crates at a version that has (g) and (h), and on the published sessions-testkit as a dev-dependency. - Domain types in paigasus-agent-host-core: the RunCommitter and Scheduler ports, and PendingToolCall as an entity with the states in (g). ### (k) Acting for a principal: named, not decided IAM has no delegation or token-exchange mechanism. An inbox records which principal it acts for. How a run carries that principal's access is the subject of SMA-793 (permissions) and SMA-794 (the credential-injecting egress proxy). This ADR does not decide it. The approver rule in (g) does not depend on it. ### (l) The Scheduler port contract - Follow-ups (one-shot) and schedules (recurring, cron plus an IANA time zone) both exist in v1 (SMA-788). - A fire produces an inbox event with a deterministic id timer:: and a fixed source. The dedup constraint then makes a double fire harmless, for any adapter. - The Postgres adapter selects due timers with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, compared with the database now(). It inserts the event and marks the follow-up done (or advances the schedule) in one transaction. - A run commit can create and cancel timers. ### (m) Event-to-input rendering One renderer turns an inbox event into model input, for the first batch and for Inject: - The output is user-role content, never system-role. - Each event is a delimited block with its type, source, time and data. The delimiters mark the content as untrusted data, not as instructions. - actorprn, correlationid and other internal attributes are not shown to the model. ### (n) Paths into the system role | Path | Rule | | --- | --- | | Agent definition (system prompt, tool descriptions) | Operator-authored. The only system-role content. | | Helikon hooks with InjectSystemMessage | The host never uses them with event, tool or memory content. | | Compacted | Projected as user-role by PgRunSession (decision (f)). | | Memory loaded at run start (SMA-789, SMA-791) | Loaded as user-role content or as tool results, never system-role. | ### (o) Observability and crash tests - Metrics: lost leases, discarded runs, attempts per event, dead events, open deferrals and their age, inbox lag (oldest claimable event age). SMA-798 owns the names. - A crash-injection test matrix for SMA-790: after a tool call and before the commit; during the commit; after the commit and before the lease release; during a heartbeat partition. - A LISTEN/NOTIFY nudge, if added later, stays outside the run commit transaction. In IAM, a full notification queue fails the COMMIT. ## Consequences Positive - A self-hoster runs the core on Postgres and NATS. Redis is optional. Temporal is not needed. - A run that lost its lease never commits, and it stops at once. - A run's session events, messages, timers, deferrals, memory changes and inbox acks commit together, or not at all. - One run serves one thread, so provider message order and the thread history stay correct. - A deferred call is a first-class outcome, bound to the args the approver saw, and only the inbox principal can approve it. - Untrusted content never enters the system role, on any of the paths in (n). - One envelope across IAM and the agent host. Trace links (SMA-798) can use the CloudEvents id. Negative and risks - Two Helikon changes, (g) and (h), and the testkit publication come before SMA-795 and before the fold and interrupt policies. A delay in Helikon delays those issues. - After a deferral is stored, the host cannot roll back below the Helikon version that has (g). - The host owns PgRunSession and host-side compaction. They must stay correct against Helikon's session semantics. The testkit reduces this risk. - A crash repeats the whole run, so a side-effect tool can run again with different args. Tool authors must know this. - Polling Postgres for due timers and new events adds load. At high volume a nudge may be needed. - The S3 memory adapter is at-least-once and can keep writes of a discarded run. - An interrupt cannot stop the outbox messages of the turn that is in flight. ## Alternatives considered - Temporal as the durability substrate. Not chosen. Self-hosters would need a Temporal cluster. TemporalRunner v0 rejects hooks, guardrails and handoffs. The Scheduler port keeps it possible. - NATS JetStream as the inbox. Not chosen. The dedup window is time-limited, a work-queue stream gives no relational view for the console or for the claimable predicate, and timers and memory still need Postgres. NATS stays an ingress source. - Redis Streams as the inbox. Not chosen. Not durable enough to be the source of truth, and ADR-0016 already rejected it for events. - Postgres advisory locks instead of a lease row. Not chosen. A session-level lock is lost with the connection, gives no fencing token, and does not work well behind a pooler. - One inbox per agent, or per thread. Not chosen. Per agent mixes principals. Per thread loses one lease per principal. - A bespoke envelope, or binary protobuf. Not chosen. ADR-0016 already uses CloudEvents JSON. Protobuf stays an upgrade path. - One run for a batch with several threads. Not chosen. It puts user messages between tool results, which providers reject, and it sends replies on the wrong thread. - A per-turn commit. Not chosen for v1. It would bound a crash to one turn. But Helikon persists only at finalize, so it needs a third Helikon change, and it makes outbox messages of earlier turns visible before the run ends. Revisit trigger. - Helikon's CompactingSession. Not chosen. It projects the summary as system-role, compacts inside append before the commit, and makes a model call that nothing can cancel. - Session: one long session per inbox. Not chosen. Unrelated events share one context and compaction loses detail more often. - Session: always fresh, except approval replies. Not chosen. A normal reply loses the conversation unless memory holds it. - Defer: deny now, re-run later and let the model retry. Not chosen. It depends on the model sending the same call again, which is not verified. - Defer: block in the process until the answer comes. Not chosen. It holds the lease and a worker slot for hours. - Approval by possession of a link token alone. Not chosen. A forwarded email would approve a dangerous call. - Mid-run: interrupt only, through CancellationToken. Not chosen. A cancel can land inside a tool call, and a side-effect tool can then run twice. - Mid-run: a hook with InjectSystemMessage. Not chosen. It puts external content into the system role. ## Revisit triggers - Temporal's Rust SDK and TemporalRunner support hooks, guardrails and handoffs. - A principal needs parallel runs (split the inbox). - Postgres polling load becomes measurable (add a nudge, outside the commit). - Repeated side effects after crashes become a real problem (per-turn commit). - Helikon gets a native user-message injection API (re-check (h)). - Approval by delegates or admins is needed (extend (g), with (k)). ## References - [SMA-785](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-785/adr-always-on-agent-host-durability-substrate-worker-model-event): this issue - Anthropic, "Building always-on agents": [https://claude.com/resources/articles/building-always-on-agents](https://claude.com/resources/articles/building-always-on-agents) - Helikon ADR-6 (durability is a seam): Library + pluggable Runner trait; durability is a seam, not built-in - ADR-0005, ADR-0006, ADR-0014, ADR-0016 - Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-18-sma-785-agent-host-adr-design.md (paigasus-core) ","cover":null,"icon":null,"full_width":false,"path":"Paigasus / Development / Architecture Decision Records","verification":{"state":"unverified"},"page_last_edited_at":"2026-11-18T19:04:36.657Z"}

content.text: I apply the round-1 and round-2 text to decision (f) on the page, with targeted replacements.

input.command: update_content

content_updates.new_str: - The resolved thread. An event's threadid resolves through successor_id to the last thread of the chain. Every rule below uses the resolved thread, never the raw threadid. A run commit sets successor_id only on a thread whose successor_id is empty, so it never overwrites an existing link. (Storing the resolved id on the event is the builder's call.) - The claimable predicate. An event is claimable when its status is pending, not_before has passed, it is not claimed by a running run under a live lease, and one of these is true for its resolved thread: - the resolved thread has no open deferred call; - the event resolves that thread's open call: an approval reply that matches an open call_id, the call's expiry timer event, or a user message on that thread (see (g), "superseded"). A stale event of an older thread in the chain does not resolve a call of its successor.

content_updates.old_str: - Claim. Take the oldest claimable event of the inbox (by received_at). - If it has a live threadid, claim the claimable events of that thread, in received_at order, up to the batch limit. The run resumes that thread. - If it has a threadid whose thread is not live, claim the claimable events with that same threadid, up to the batch limit. The run starts a fresh session under a new thread. Events of two different expired threads never share a run. - If it has no threadid (or the host dropped it, decision (e)), claim the claimable events that have no threadid, up to the batch limit. The run starts a fresh session under a new thread. - Events of other threads stay pending for the next claim. So several messages in one thread still produce one reply, and no run mixes threads.
content_updates.new_str: - Claim. Take the oldest claimable event of the inbox (by received_at). Group and order events by their resolved thread. - If its resolved thread is live, claim the claimable events with the same resolved thread, in received_at order, up to the batch limit. The run resumes that thread. - If its resolved thread is not live, claim the claimable events with the same resolved thread, up to the batch limit. The run starts a fresh session under a new thread, and the run commit sets successor_id on the resolved thread to the new thread. Events of two different expired threads never share a run. The rest of a backlog larger than the batch limit then resolves to the new thread and keeps its session history. - If it has no threadid (or the host dropped it, decision (e)), claim the claimable events that have no threadid, up to the batch limit. The run starts a fresh session under a new thread. If more such events wait than the batch limit, each batch is a separate session on purpose: an event with no threadid does not continue earlier work. - Events of other resolved threads stay pending for the next claim. So several messages in one thread still produce one reply, and no run mixes threads.
